ch11.note: The parting song of the assassin Jing Ke, who in 227 BC set out to kill the king of Qin knowing he would not return: "The wind blows chill, the Yi River is cold; once the brave man leaves, he comes back no more." Wu Shi recites it on the eve of a mission he expects will cost his life.

ch11.anchor: In East China there was the martyr Li Bai
ch11.note: Li Bai (no relation to the Tang poet) was a Communist radio operator in Shanghai, seized and executed just before the city fell in 1949. His story became the celebrated film The Unfailing Radio Wave.

ch11.anchor: the rape of the Peking University student Shen Chong
ch11.note: The Shen Chong incident: the rape of a Peking University student by U.S. Marines in Beiping on Christmas Eve 1946 touched off nationwide anti-American student protests, which the Communists turned into a "second front" in the cities.

ch11.anchor: beat back Lin Biao's forces at the battle of Siping
ch11.note: At Siping in 1947 Chen Mingren's stubborn defense inflicted heavy losses on Lin Biao's army, one of the rare Nationalist successes of the Northeast war. Two years later Chen led his troops over to the Communists in Hunan, the propaganda value of a Central Army general defecting being the point the author makes here.

ch11.anchor: used fellow-townsman ties to recruit Liu Jinchang
ch11.note: The source names both the Nationalist Baoding station chief and the deserter he recruits "Liu Jinchang." This is almost certainly a slip in the original; the two are distinct people. Rendered as printed.

ch13.anchor: set up a National Security Commission
ch13.note: The Central National Security Commission, established in 2013 under Party general secretary Xi Jinping, consolidating oversight of internal and external security. The book's second edition, from which this afterword comes, was written in its wake.
Qiangli jigou, the “organs of force” or “power organs”: the army, police, and security services, the coercive arms of the state; the phrase parallels the Russian siloviki.

ch13.anchor: the founding of the state on September 30, 1949
ch13.note: The People's Republic was proclaimed on October 1, 1949; September 30 was the close of the first Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, which elected the new government. The author dates the founding from that eve.

ch13.anchor: the crushing of the "Gang of Four"
ch13.note: Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen, the radical leadership faction blamed for the Cultural Revolution, arrested in October 1976, a month after Mao's death.

ch12.anchor: three days' free plunder
ch12.note: When Zeng Guofan's Hunan Army stormed Nanjing (Tianjing), the capital of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, in 1864, the victorious troops sacked the city. Da suo san ri (“a great search of three days”) was the customary license to loot a captured city.

ch12.anchor: jokingly called "the Hundred-and-Eight Heroes."
ch12.note: An allusion to Shuihu zhuan (Water Margin), the classic novel whose 108 outlaw-heroes gather at the marsh stronghold of Liangshan. The 101 trainees plus 7 instructors made 108. In the roster, “(f.)” marks the trainees the source flags as women (女), whose given names do not otherwise show gender in romanization.

ch12.anchor: reactionary party, corps, and agent organizations
ch12.note: “Party and corps” renders dang-tuan: the Nationalist Party (Kuomintang) and its Three People's Principles Youth Corps, whose members were registered and screened by the new authorities after the takeover.

ch12.anchor: the rinsed mutton of the Donglaishun
ch12.note: The Donglaishun, a celebrated Beijing restaurant founded in 1903 and famous for shuan yangrou, thin-sliced mutton rinsed briefly in a communal pot of simmering broth.

ch12.anchor: poking fun at the Yiguandao
ch12.note: The Yiguandao (“Way of Pervading Unity”), a popular syncretic religious sect with a mass following, banned and violently suppressed as a “reactionary secret society” in the campaigns of 1950–1951.

ch12.anchor: The French military attaché, Lei Meng
ch12.note: The French military attaché's name survives here only in Chinese transliteration (雷蒙, Lei Meng); his name in French is not established, so the romanization is provisional.

ch12.anchor: Farewell, Leighton Stuart!
ch12.note: John Leighton Stuart (1876–1962), American missionary-educator, founding president of Yenching University, and U.S. ambassador to China from 1946 to 1949. Mao's essay “Farewell, Leighton Stuart!” (August 1949) mocked him as the embodiment of a failed American China policy; it long remained a set text in Chinese schools.

ch12.anchor: contact with the Panchen Lama's establishment
ch12.note: The tenth Panchen Lama (1938–1989), the second-ranking figure of Tibetan Buddhism after the Dalai Lama, whose seat was then at Xiangride in Qinghai. The xingyuan was his personal establishment or court; the Kashag was the governing council of the Tibetan government in Lhasa.

ch12.anchor: granted the rank of Senior General in 1955
ch12.note: In the People's Liberation Army ranks conferred in 1955, da jiang (“Senior General”) stood just below marshal; ten officers held it. It outranked shang jiang (“General”), the rank later cited for Li Kenong.

ch12.anchor: "the Eight Vajra Warriors."
ch12.note: Ba da jingang, the eight guardian-warrior kings of Buddhist iconography; used here half in jest for the ministry's eight formidable deputy ministers.

ch12.anchor: earliest "counter-terror" rule anywhere in the world
ch12.note: The author's claim, and a rhetorical one. No external scholarship treats a 1950 internal CCP intelligence guideline as the world's first counter-terrorism measure, and “counter-terrorism” in the modern sense is anachronistic here. UNCORROBORATED; the passage reflects the author's framing, written after the 2001 attacks, rather than a documented first.

ch12.anchor: Light and dark had changed places
ch12.note: The chapter's title, ming an yi wei: the “light” (the open, the state) and the “dark” (the hidden, the clandestine services) trade places, as the Party's once-secret apparatus comes into the open as the public-security organs of a ruling state and, in the campaigns that follow, is turned against its own.

ch12.anchor: the great Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries
ch12.note: The zhenfan campaign of 1950–1953, which the author presents here as a triumph of public order. Its scale was far bloodier than the text lets on: deputy public-security minister Xu Zirong's 1954 report counted about 712,000 executed, 1,290,000 imprisoned, and 1,200,000 placed under control; Mao himself later spoke of some 700,000 killed. Historians' estimates of the executions run from about 500,000–720,000 at the low end to two or three million. CORROBORATED as a mass campaign of execution; the book's framing omits the toll.

ch12.anchor: China became the safest great country in the world.
ch12.note: The author's partisan verdict. Low reported ordinary crime in the Mao years coexisted with waves of state-driven political violence — the very campaigns and purges this chapter goes on to describe — so “safest” measures only one kind of safety. The judgment is the author's, not a neutral finding.

ch12.anchor: the new China's first unjust, false, and wrongful case
ch12.note: On Pan Hannian, see the notes at Chapters 2 and 9. He and the Shanghai police chief Yang Fan were arrested in 1955 and both were posthumously rehabilitated in the 1980s. That the author — himself a sympathetic insider — flatly calls these “unjust, false, and wrongful cases” reflects the settled post-Mao verdict.

ch12.anchor: Toppling "Peng, Luo, Lu, and Yang"
ch12.note: Peng Zhen, Luo Ruiqing, Lu Dingyi, and Yang Shangkun, four senior officials purged together in 1965–66 as the “Peng-Luo-Lu-Yang anti-Party clique,” an opening move of the Cultural Revolution.

ch12.anchor: Smash the police, procuratorate, and courts!
ch12.note: The Cultural Revolution slogan za lan gong-jian-fa: smash the gong (public security, the police), the jian (the procuratorate), and the fa (the courts). Mao spoke of having the legal apparatus “beaten to a pulp”; from 1967 the procuratorate and courts effectively collapsed and the security leadership was purged wholesale. CORROBORATED as to the slogan and the wholesale purge; the casualty figures that follow are the public-security system's own post-Mao reckoning.

ch12.anchor: excavating a cultural gene
ch12.note: The book's closing figure, which answers the mining metaphor of its Preface: the “cultural gene” is the inherited character — the habits, methods, and instincts — that the author sees carried down through the Communists' intelligence tradition. The image is his own, meant as heritage rather than biology.

ch12.anchor: the Asian-African Conference
ch12.note: The 1955 Bandung Conference. En route, an Air India plane, the Kashmir Princess, chartered for the Chinese delegation, was destroyed by a bomb planted by a Nationalist agent; sixteen people died, but Zhou Enlai had changed his travel plans and was not aboard.

ch12.anchor: won back the returning "acting president."
ch12.note: Li Zongren (see above in this chapter), who had been the Republic of China's acting president in 1949, returned to the mainland from exile in the United States in 1965, a propaganda coup the CCP's united-front and intelligence organs worked to bring about.

ch12.anchor: the greatest spy has no name
ch12.note: The first two clauses adapt Laozi (Daodejing, ch. 41): “the greatest sound is faint of voice, the greatest form has no shape” (see the note at Chapter 6). “The greatest spy has no name” is the author's own coinage completing the parallel.
